notes: Pheretima posthuma (earthworm): annelid (segmented worm); ~10–15 cm long; ~100–150 segments.
External features: clitellum (segments 15–31 in Pheretima) for reproduction; setae (bristles) on each segment for anchoring; chaetae; prostomium (first segment, sensory).
Body wall: cuticle + circular and longitudinal muscles; coelom (true body cavity) with coelomic fluid; septa between segments.
Habitat: moist soil; night-active; breathes through the skin (cutaneous respiration).
Significance: aerates soil, adds humus, improves soil structure and fertility; a key invertebrate studied in NEB.
Taxonomy: Animalia > Annelida > Clitellata > Haplotaxida (Lumbricidae) > Pheretima.
NEB focus: external anatomy, general body plan, and habitat of Pheretima.
confusion: Earthworms are Annelids, NOT arthropods; they have a soft body with setae, not a hard exoskeleton.
The clitellum is a thickened, saddle-like region used to form the cocoon — it is NOT a reproductive organ itself.
Earthworms have a closed circulatory system (blood vessels + heart-like vessels), not an open one.
Respiration is through the moist skin (cutaneous); there are no gills or lungs.
Earthworms are hermaphrodites (both male and female organs) but exchange sperm with another worm (cross-fertilisation).
Segments are called "metameres"; each has a set of setae for anchoring during locomotion.

universalFacts: A single gram of soil can contain several earthworms; they turn over a significant fraction of topsoil each year.
Earthworms are the most commonly used model annelid in school laboratories.
Earthworms are hermaphrodites but usually cross-fertilise with another individual.
examples: Pheretima posthuma — the Indian earthworm model; clitellum on segments 15–31.
Lumbricus terrestris — the European garden worm; used in many textbooks.
The setae (bristles) on each segment provide grip during peristaltic locomotion.
The clitellum (segments 15–31) secretes the cocoon that encloses the eggs.
